text: Prophets of Da City (POC) is a hip hop crew from Cape Town, South Africa, consisting of about eight members, including Ishmael Morabe (vocals), Mark Heuvel (dance), Shaheen Ariefdien, Ramone, and DJ Ready D, with fluctuating membership. Their music blends hip hop, reggae, and traditional African rhythms. The group's albums are Our World (1990), Boom Style (1992), Age of Truth (1993), Phunk Phlow (1994), Universal Souljaz (1995), and Ghetto Code (1997). They are currently signed to the independent record label Ghetto Ruff. POC began in late 1988 when Shaheen and Ready D produced a demo in an 8-track studio owned by Shaheen's father, Issy Ariefdien, and Lance Stehr, the current Ghetoruff CEO, which became "Our World" (1990), South Africa’s first hip hop album. The album featured the first recorded Cape slang hip-hop song, "Dala Flat" (do it thoroughly), an uptempo goema-inspired "Stop the Violence," and a hip house meets mbaqanga title track, along with "Roots" inspired by Abdullah Ibrahim and featuring DJ A-ski. Despite its innovative Cape Town influences, record labels rejected it due to its social commentary, favoring party-oriented music. Lance, the group’s manager, established Ku-shu shu Records and secured a distribution and marketing deal with Teal Trutone (Gallo subsidiary). In 1990, POC was nominated for the OKTV Award for Best New Group and launched an 80-leg anti-drug school tour reaching an average of 70,000 students. Their 1991 release, Boom Style, referenced the TR-808 drum machine’s punch and was criticized for mocking the Afrikaner national anthem "Die Stem" and colonial icons, leading to a formal complaint from the censorship board. The album included the song "Ons Stem" (our voice), a response to "die stem," and "Hard Time on Stage," a follow-up to "Murder on Stage." The group’s live shows incorporated turntablism, breakdancing, and aerosol art to promote hip hop culture. The "Kicking Non Stop" video was censored after members placed a portrait of then-president P. W. Botha in a fridge. In 1992, POC performed at the Montreux Jazz Festival in Switzerland with Quincy Jones and Caiphus Semenya, launched an anti-drug campaign in Namibia covering 65 schools, and began facilitating workshops on deejaying, b-boying, and hip hop writing. Leading up to South Africa’s first democratic election, they conducted a national voter education campaign. Issy Ariefdien contributed to production since the first album, and the group brought in former rival Patrick Hickey, a.k.a. Caramel, for the Age of Truth album. In 1993, POC performed at the Visions of Africa music festival in Denmark and conducted a national voter education tour in high schools, community centres, and universities. Their performance at Nelson Mandela’s inauguration in 1994, where they sang "Excellent, finally black President," was a significant milestone, especially as the members grew up during apartheid and saw it as a triumph over racial barriers and a moment when hip hop entered the mainstream. Mark Schwartz notes that in 1985, Ready and Shaheen responded to a military crackdown in Mitchell’s Plain by taking up bricks and gasoline bombs, and over the next nine years, they persisted until performing at Mandela’s inauguration. In 2006, student filmmakers Sean Drummond and Dylan Valley located the group members, and the documentary *Lost Prophets* was screened at South African film festivals. In 2015, POC celebrated 20 years since the release of *Our World*. Age of Truth (1993), inspired by the Bomb Squad (Public Enemy) and Boogiemen (Ice Cube), is considered their most militant and musically daring album and South Africa’s first hip hop classic, though most songs were banned. The song "Understand Where I'm Coming From" addresses poverty, social dislocation, and questions patriotism in a class-stratified society, with lyrics like "Why should I fight for a country's glory / When it ignores me? / Besides, the township's already a war zone / So why complain or moan?" It also reflects on the persistence of racial and class inequalities post-apartheid. The song was included in the Tommy Boy Planet Rap album, recorded and mixed at Bop Studios in Bophutatswana, where the head engineer offered a reduced rate to attract big stars and legitimize the Bantustan. POC learned of this intent and included the line "Fuck Mangope (Bophutatswana's head of fake state) even if we record here," prompting the engineer to confiscate the mixed DATs and confront the group. After a heated debate, POC left with a 'stolen' backup copy that became the released version. POC’s music frequently addresses socio-political issues in South Africa’s economically depressed urban areas. According to "Globalization and Gangster Rap: Hip Hop in the Post-Apartheid City," "Understand Where I'm Coming From" is a lament about poverty and social dislocation, questioning patriotism in a stratified society. The song reflects how young African and Coloured youth see hip hop as the art form that best expresses economic marginality and social dislocation. Similar to American politically conscious hip hop, POC’s work expresses rebellion and separation from the central government. In "Dallah Flet 2," negative and misogynistic attitudes toward single mothers are rapped, a theme Zine Magubane identifies as common in American rap. A 2001 article by Adam Haupt, “Black Thing: Hip-Hop Nationalism, ‘Race’ and Gender in Prophets of da City and Brasse vannie Kaap,” argues that gender-based issues on Age of Truth stem from the crew’s black nationalist politics, which often privileged patriarchal structures and marginalized women. Haupt’s analysis in *Stealing Empire* positions POC’s work closer to black nationalist US hip hop of the late 80s and 90s than to gangsta rap. The article also corrects a misattribution, crediting the Black Consciousness song "Black Thing" to POC, not Black Noise. The group has also performed with notable artists such as James Brown, Public Enemy, The Fugees, Ice-T, and Quincy Jones.
